s1.title: What a Solar BOQ Actually Controls

s2.title: The 8 Mandatory Sections of a Solar Project BOQ

s3.title: The 6 BOQ Mistakes That Cost EPC Firms the Most

s5.title: What a BOQ Pricing Error Actually Costs

whoFor.label: Who this is for:
whoFor.body: EPC project managers, procurement heads and bid teams at solar contracting firms preparing BOQs for SECI, NTPC, state DISCOM, PM-KUSUM or PM Surya Ghar tenders, and for private C&I projects in India.

intro.p1: A solar project's BOQ — Bill of Quantities — is the document that decides whether your bid wins or bleeds. It converts your engineering design into a measurable price schedule: every panel, cable, structure and earthing rod listed with quantity, unit and specification. Get it right and you win at a margin that survives procurement. Get it wrong and you absorb overruns that can erase months of project profit in a single purchase order.
intro.p2: Yet most EPC firms — especially those scaling from rooftop to ground-mount, or from 1 MW to 10 MW — still prepare BOQs using rough estimates, copied templates, or last project's numbers updated by feel. With EPC margins in India running at 5–9% of contract value, a 3% error across the total BOQ takes roughly 40% of a 7% margin with it. That is not a rounding difference. That is the year.
intro.p3: This guide gives you the complete framework: what every section of a solar BOQ must contain, the line items contractors routinely leave out, the compliance requirements that can invalidate a BOQ in government tenders, and a pre-submission checklist to run before every bid.

scenario.label: Real-world scenario
scenario.quote: We won a 5 MW DISCOM tender in MP. The BOQ had DC cable calculated by straight-line distance — not actual cable run with routing, elevation and termination allowance. By the time we ordered we were 18% short on cable volume. Emergency procurement at spot prices cost us ₹14 lakh over budget. The margin on that project went from 7% to under 5%.
scenario.attribution: — Project Manager, mid-size EPC firm, Central India (2025)

solarBoq.s1p1: A Bill of Quantities is a structured document listing every material, component and work item needed to complete an installation, with unit of measurement, quantity and specification. In Indian solar tenders — SECI, NTPC, state DISCOM, PM-KUSUM, PM Surya Ghar — the BOQ is the foundation of competitive bidding. Every contractor prices the same BOQ, which is what makes bids comparable.
solarBoq.s1p2: But the BOQ does far more than win tenders. It drives your entire procurement cycle. Purchase orders are raised against BOQ line items. Site deliveries are tracked against BOQ quantities. Progress billing is certified against BOQ milestones. Retention and final settlement are computed from it. A weak BOQ does not just lose tenders — it creates procurement chaos across the whole project lifecycle and hands the client the stronger position in every variation discussion.
solarBoq.s1quote: A well-built solar BOQ is not a spreadsheet. It is an engineering document that determines whether the project makes money or loses it — before a single panel is ordered.
solarBoq.s2p1: A complete solar BOQ covers eight distinct categories. Missing any one creates a procurement gap that shows up later as a cost overrun, a delay, or a failed inspection. Section 8 — statutory, insurance and commercial items — is the one most often absent altogether, because it does not look like "material".

boqSections.title: Solar PV Modules
boqSections.sub: The most compliance-sensitive section in the entire BOQ

rows.item: Solar PV module — state technology (TOPCon / Mono PERC / bifacial) and exact model code
rows.spec: Wp, V<sub>oc</sub>, I<sub>sc</sub>, temperature coefficient, efficiency, bifaciality factor

rows.item: Module type & safety certification
rows.spec: IEC 61215 design qualification; IEC 61730-1/-2 safety

rows.item: PID resistance declaration
rows.spec: IEC TS 62804-1 test report

rows.item: Salt-mist / ammonia resistance (coastal or agri sites)
Performance warranty documentation
rows.spec: Linear output warranty, ≥80% at year 25; product warranty separately stated
rows.flag: Confirm at order, not at bid

rows.item: ALMM List-II cell-origin declaration + cell traceability
rows.spec: Cell manufacturer, List-II reference, batch traceability

rows.item: DCR certificate (where the scheme requires it)
rows.spec: NISE DCR portal reference
rows.flag: PM Surya Ghar, KUSUM B & C, CPSU-II

boqSections.title: Inverters and Power Conversion
boqSections.sub: String, central or micro — and BIS, not just IEC

rows.item: String / central inverter — state kW rating, phase, DC:AC ratio
rows.spec: Euro or CEC weighted efficiency, MPPT count and voltage window, THD limit

rows.item: BIS registration for the inverter model
rows.spec: IS 16221 Parts 1 & 2, IS 16169

rows.item: Grid-interface protection settings & compliance report
rows.spec: Anti-islanding, LVRT/HVRT, frequency ride-through

rows.item: Inverter mounting structure / room / platform
rows.spec: Weather-rated enclosure, IP65 minimum, ventilation or forced cooling

rows.item: Remote monitoring / SCADA integration
rows.spec: Modbus TCP / SunSpec, data logging interval, remote access provision

rows.item: AC output cable — inverter to ACDB
rows.spec: Sized from load and voltage-drop calculation

rows.item: Auxiliary supply / UPS for SCADA and control
rows.spec: Backup duration as per O&M spec

boqSections.title: Module Mounting Structures
boqSections.sub: Fixed tilt or tracker — the design must be site-specific

rows.item: GI / aluminium mounting structure — state tilt angle and row pitch
rows.spec: Hot-dip galvanised, coating thickness stated in microns (typically 80 µm)

rows.item: Foundation bolts / pull bolts / chemical anchors
rows.spec: SS 304/316 or HDG grade, pull-out capacity stated

rows.item: Mid clamps / end clamps
rows.spec: Anodised aluminium, matched to the module frame thickness

rows.item: Wind load design certificate
rows.spec: Site wind zone, basic wind speed, terrain category

rows.item: Tracker drive, controller and backtracking system (if applicable)
rows.spec: Motor, gearbox, controller, stow strategy

rows.item: Structure earthing bonding jumpers
rows.spec: Tinned copper braid or GI, table-to-table continuity
rows.flag: Often merged into earthing and lost

boqSections.title: DC-Side Balance of System
boqSections.sub: The most error-prone section — measure, never estimate

rows.item: DC solar cable — string wiring
rows.spec: 4 / 6 mm² as calculated, 1.5 kV DC rated, UV and ozone resistant, TÜV certified

rows.item: DC main / array cable to combiner and inverter
rows.spec: Cross-section from current and voltage-drop calculation, not from precedent

rows.item: MC4 / T4 connectors
rows.spec: IP68, 1.5 kV DC, single-brand mating only

rows.item: DC combiner box / string monitoring unit
rows.spec: Fuse per string, DC isolator, SPD, IP65 minimum

rows.item: DC cable tray, conduit or underground duct
rows.spec: HDPE or perforated GI tray as per layout

rows.item: Surge protection device, DC side (Type II)
rows.spec: Rated for maximum string V<sub>oc</sub> at lowest site temperature

rows.item: Cable ties, glands, labels, ferrules and marking
rows.spec: UV-stabilised ties; permanent cable identification
rows.flag: Small line, real cost at scale

boqSections.title: AC-Side Electrical and Evacuation
boqSections.sub: Grid connectivity, metering and the HT items small BOQs forget

rows.item: AC distribution board (ACDB)
rows.spec: MCCB rated, IP54 minimum, busbar rating stated

rows.item: AC power cable — inverter to transformer / grid
rows.spec: Armoured XLPE, cross-section from load and derating factors

rows.item: Step-up transformer
rows.spec: kVA rating, vector group, CRGO core, losses guaranteed

rows.item: HT panel / RMU / VCB with protection relays
rows.spec: Rated voltage and breaking capacity; numerical relay

rows.item: HT cable, terminations and jointing kits
rows.spec: Heat-shrink or cold-shrink kits, quantity per termination

rows.item: CT/PT metering cubicle and ABT / special energy meter
rows.spec: Accuracy class, DISCOM-approved make

rows.item: Net meter / bi-directional energy meter
rows.spec: DISCOM-approved make, ToD capable where required

rows.item: AC surge protection device (Type I / II)
rows.spec: Rated for AC bus voltage and expected surge exposure

rows.item: Evacuation line — poles, conductor, insulators, right of way
rows.spec: As per DISCOM sanction letter
rows.flag: A whole scope, not a line

boqSections.title: Earthing, Lightning Protection and Safety
boqSections.sub: The most under-specified section in contractor BOQs

rows.item: Earth electrodes / pits — equipment and structure earthing
rows.spec: Copper-bonded rod or GI plate; count and depth derived from the earthing design and measured soil resistivity

rows.item: Earth ring conductor
rows.spec: 25×4 mm GI flat or equivalent copper; measure the full ring from the earthing layout

rows.item: Soil resistivity test and earth resistance test report
rows.spec: Four-probe test before design

rows.item: Lightning protection system
rows.spec: Conventional air terminals, down conductors and dedicated earth per IS/IEC 62305; if an ESE terminal is proposed it is governed by NF C 17-102, not IEC 62305
rows.flag: Need established by IEC 62305-2 risk assessment, not by plant size

rows.item: Safety kit — rubber mats, danger boards, shock-treatment chart, first-aid box, sand buckets, CO₂ / DCP extinguishers
rows.spec: As per CEA safety regulations
rows.flag: Often billed as lumpsum and under-costed

rows.item: Perimeter fencing and gates
rows.spec: GI chain link, barbed wire or wall as per site

rows.item: CCTV, anti-theft fasteners, security cabin
rows.spec: Camera count and recording retention

boqSections.title: Civil Works, Monitoring and O&M Infrastructure

rows.item: Foundations / plinths — module rows, inverter room, control panel
rows.spec: Concrete grade per structural drawing, PCC and reinforcement separately

rows.item: Cable trench excavation, sand bedding, brick protection and backfill
rows.spec: Depth and profile per cable layout drawing

rows.item: Site grading, approach road, drainage and culverts
rows.spec: As per topographic survey

rows.item: Weather monitoring station
rows.spec: Pyranometer (POA + GHI), module and ambient temperature sensors, anemometer

rows.item: SCADA / remote monitoring infrastructure
rows.spec: Web-based, logging interval stated, data retention period

rows.item: Module cleaning system and water source
rows.spec: Manual, semi-automatic or robotic; plus borewell or tank, pump and piping
rows.flag: Water source is a real cost, not an assumption

rows.item: Mandatory spares for the O&M period
rows.spec: Spares list as specified in the tender

rows.item: Commissioning, testing and documentation
rows.spec: Pre-commissioning tests, PAC/SAC, O&M manuals, as-built drawings, training
rows.flag: Required for handover and release of retention

boqSections.title: Statutory, Commercial and Risk Items
boqSections.sub: The section most BOQs do not have at all

rows.item: Electrical Inspector / CEIG approval and drawing charges
rows.spec: Statutory fees, drawing submission, inspection

rows.item: DISCOM connectivity, supervision and net-metering charges
rows.spec: Application, feasibility, supervision and testing fees

rows.item: Insurance — erection all-risk, transit, third-party
rows.spec: Cover from despatch to PAC, plus the O&M period

rows.item: Freight, unloading, internal shifting and storage
rows.spec: Including module handling and site warehousing

rows.item: Third-party inspection and factory acceptance testing
rows.spec: Inspection agency charges, travel, witness testing

rows.item: Bank guarantees — EMD, performance, advance
rows.spec: Commission plus margin money blocked for the tenor
rows.flag: A financing cost, price it as one

rows.item: GST treatment
rows.spec: Concessional rate on the goods portion, standard rate on services; state the split you have assumed

rows.item: Price variation / escalation clause
rows.spec: Whether module, copper and steel movement is passed through
rows.flag: If absent, you carry the commodity risk

rows.item: Energy storage (where mandated)
rows.spec: Battery racks, PCS, EMS/BMS, HVAC, fire suppression, containerisation

solarBoq.moduleNote: Do not price modules as one line. Split DCR and non-DCR, because the gap is enormous: JMK Research put domestic non-DCR TOPCon at ₹14.2/Wp in April 2026 against DCR TOPCon at ₹22.3/Wp — and DCR TOPCon then rose 9.4% month-on-month in May.
solarBoq.cableNote: Rule of thumb for cable: routed length typically runs 1.15–1.25× the straight-line SLD distance once you add elevation, obstacle routing and termination loops. Use the cable schedule as the source document — the ratio above is a sanity check, not a substitute for it.

almm.label: ⚠ ALMM position as on 3 August 2026 — read before finalising modules
items: ALMM List-II (cells) came into force 1 June 2026. MNRE's O.M. dated 18 July 2026 gave net-metering and open-access projects a limited window: commission on or before 31 December 2026 and List-II does not apply. This is a transition window, not a rollback — there is no blanket extension.

The 4 August 2026 clarification is the one most BOQs still ignore. Competitively bid projects with bid submission on or before 31 August 2025 stay exempt from List-II; anything bid after that date must comply. For rooftop on government buildings, the exempt bid windows are on/before 9 Dec 2024, or 28 Jul 2025 to 31 Aug 2025.
PM Surya Ghar residential net metering is exempt from List-II until 31 March 2027, provided the application went through the national portal. List-I still applies.
Behind-the-meter captive: private consumers are outside both lists. Government and PSU captive projects must use List-I modules now, with List-II cells applying after 31 Dec 2026.

ALMM List-I remains mandatory for all government, government-assisted, scheme-linked, open-access and net-metering projects — and it is enforced at model level. "Waaree 540 W" is not a specification; the exact model code is.

Plan for List-III. ALMM for ingots and wafers takes effect 1 June 2028, with the first list published once at least three independent manufacturers with a combined 15 GW are operational. Long-tenor EPC and RESCO contracts signed today will cross that date.
DCR is a separate test from ALMM. MNRE has confirmed the List-II orders do not change DCR provisions. A module can be List-I listed and still fail DCR.

midCta.title: Source BOQ-ready solar equipment from verified suppliers
midCta.desc: Headsup B2B maps your BOQ line items to ALMM-compliant, BIS-certified products from 1,000+ verified suppliers — with pan-India delivery and 60-day procurement credit.

mistakes.title: Estimating DC cable by SLD distance, not actual run
mistakes.body: Single-line diagrams show electrical connectivity, not physical routing. Actual run includes elevation, routing around structures and loop allowance at every termination.
mistakes.impact: Typical overrun: 15–25% more cable than the BOQ carries

mistakes.title: Naming the manufacturer instead of the ALMM model code
mistakes.body: ALMM is enforced model by model. "Waaree 540 W" is not sufficient — the BOQ must carry the exact List-I model code, and a model quoted at bid stage may be delisted by the time you procure.

mistakes.title: Missing the earthing conductor ring measurement
mistakes.body: Most BOQs list earth pits correctly but understate the GI flat ring that connects them. For a 1 MW array the ring alone can run 500–700 m, plus the electrodes it serves.
mistakes.impact: Typical overrun: ₹0.7–1.5L on a 1 MW project

mistakes.title: Leaving SCADA and monitoring out of the BOQ
mistakes.body: Remote monitoring, SCADA and the weather station are mandatory in SECI, NTPC and most DISCOM contracts. Added later as a variation, they become a negotiation you will lose.
mistakes.impact: Typical addition: ₹4–12L depending on project size

mistakes.title: Reusing last project's cable specification
mistakes.body: Cable cross-section follows current and permissible voltage drop, not project size. A longer string run or higher ambient on a new site can push you from 4 mm² to 6 mm².
mistakes.impact: Consequence: overheating, inverter trips, warranty exposure

mistakes.title: Omitting civil and statutory quantities from the electrical BOQ
mistakes.body: Trench excavation, foundation concrete, cleaning water source, CEIG fees and DISCOM charges get split into a "separate" BOQ — and then forgotten in the cost estimate entirely.
mistakes.impact: Typical overrun: ₹8–20L on a 5 MW project

steps.title: Lock the engineering design before starting the BOQ
steps.body: A BOQ built on a preliminary design is a liability. The single-line diagram, layout plan, string sizing, earthing layout and cable schedule must all be finalised and signed off first. Design changes after BOQ submission become variation disputes.

steps.title: Use the cable schedule — never the SLD — for cable quantities
steps.body: The cable schedule lists every run with routed length, cross-section and termination allowance. It is the source document for the DC and AC cable BOQ. If the cable schedule does not exist yet, the BOQ is not ready.

steps.title: Verify ALMM status for every model on the day you submit
steps.body: Check the live MNRE portal, not a cached list, for every module model in the BOQ, and record the revision date against the line item. Keep a pre-approved alternative for each model in case of delisting between bid and procurement.

steps.title: Price against current market rates, not last quarter's POs
steps.body: Domestic DCR TOPCon module prices moved from roughly ₹27/Wp in January 2026 to ₹22/Wp in April, then rose again in May. Copper tracks LME; structure steel tracks domestic HRC and zinc. Reprice, every bid.

steps.title: Add a 3–5% procurement contingency on BoS — and hold it
steps.body: Module and inverter quantities are exact. Cables, connectors, clamps and fasteners are not: allow 3–5% for wastage, measurement variance and site conditions. This protects margin without moving your bid price materially.

steps.title: Cross-check line-by-line against the tender BOQ before submission
steps.body: Most government tenders issue their own BOQ format. Any item in the tender BOQ that is absent from your internal BOQ is a gap that converts into a cost overrun the day you win.

steps.title: Map every BOQ line to a PO line before mobilisation
steps.body: If a BOQ item has no owner, no vendor and no lead time attached to it, it will be procured late and at spot price. The BOQ-to-PO map is what turns the document into a procurement plan.

costCard.label: BOQ error cost analysis — 5 MW ground-mount solar project

rows.label: Total project value
Target EPC margin (7%)
DC cable underestimated 18%, made up at spot prices
Earthing ring conductor and electrodes missed
SCADA and weather station added as a variation, negotiated down
Civil works — trench, foundations, cleaning water — understated

solarBoq.s5p1: Four ordinary BOQ errors — none of them exotic — take margin from 7% to under 5% on a single project. Run four or five similar projects a year with the same gaps and that is ₹1.5–2 crore of avoidable margin erosion annually. That is the real cost of a weak BOQ process, and it compounds quietly because no single line item ever looks large enough to escalate.
solarBoq.s6p1: Run every bid through this before it goes out. It takes about 30 minutes.

checklist.label: Modules:
checklist.body: exact ALMM List-I model code included, BIS registration confirmed, DCR status stated, performance and product warranties separated.

checklist.label: ALMM List-II:
checklist.body: project category identified (bid date, commissioning date, net metering / open access / captive), exemption position documented in writing.

checklist.label: Inverters:
checklist.body: IEC 62109 certification and IS 16221 / IS 16169 BIS registration confirmed, grid-protection settings referenced, SCADA compatibility noted.

checklist.label: DC cable:
checklist.body: quantities taken from the cable schedule, cross-section calculated from current and voltage drop, wastage allowance added.

checklist.label: Mounting structures:
checklist.body: wind-zone-matched structural design, IS 2062 grade and galvanising thickness specified, foundation bolt material confirmed.

checklist.label: Earthing:
checklist.body: electrode count derived from soil resistivity test, ring conductor measured from the earthing layout drawing, IS 3043 compliance stated.

checklist.label: Lightning protection:
checklist.body: need established by an IEC 62305-2 risk assessment; if an ESE terminal is offered, the governing standard is stated correctly.

checklist.label: AC and HT side:
checklist.body: transformer, RMU/HT panel, termination kits, CT/PT cubicle and DISCOM-approved meter all included; evacuation line scoped.

checklist.label: Monitoring:
checklist.body: SCADA and weather station in the BOQ, logging interval and data retention specified, remote access provision confirmed.

checklist.label: Civil works:
checklist.body: trench quantities from the layout drawing, foundation concrete from the structural design, grading and approach road included, cleaning water source priced.

checklist.label: Statutory and commercial:
checklist.body: CEIG and DISCOM charges, insurance, freight, third-party inspection, bank guarantee cost and GST split all carried as line items.

checklist.label: Commissioning:
checklist.body: testing, PAC/SAC documentation, O&M manuals, as-built drawings and mandatory spares included as priced items.

checklist.label: Pricing:
checklist.body: every rate verified against current market prices — not last quarter's POs or last project's invoices — and a price-variation position taken.

checklist.label: Tender alignment:
checklist.body: your BOQ cross-checked line-by-line against the issued tender BOQ, with no missing items and no unpriced provisional sums.

takeaways.title: A solar BOQ has eight sections, not six.
takeaways.body: Modules and inverters get specified carefully. Earthing conductors, monitoring, civil works, commissioning documentation and the entire statutory-and-commercial block are routinely thin or absent.

takeaways.title: Measure cables — never estimate them.
takeaways.body: The single largest source of BOQ overruns is DC cable quantities taken from SLD distance instead of the cable schedule. Routed length typically runs 15–25% above the straight line.

takeaways.title: ALMM compliance is model-level, and the rules changed twice this year.
takeaways.body: Your BOQ must reference the exact List-I model code, and your List-II position depends on bid date, commissioning date and project category after MNRE's 18 July and 4 August 2026 orders.

takeaways.title: BOQ errors compound across a portfolio.
takeaways.body: A 2% error on an ₹18 crore project is ₹36 lakh. Four projects a year with the same gaps is ₹1.4 crore given away — invisibly, one line item at a time.

takeaways.title: Price against current rates, and say so in the bid.
takeaways.body: DCR module prices moved by double digits inside a single quarter in 2026. A BOQ priced on last year's rates is a margin risk before procurement even begins; a price-variation clause is how you stop carrying that risk alone.

faqs.q: How many sections must a solar BOQ have?
faqs.a: Eight — modules, inverters and power conversion, module mounting structures, DC-side balance of system, AC-side electrical and evacuation, earthing and lightning protection, civil works and O&M infrastructure, and statutory/commercial/risk items. The last one is the section most BOQs omit entirely, because it does not look like material.

faqs.q: Can I calculate DC cable quantity from the single-line diagram?
faqs.a: No. The SLD shows electrical connectivity, not physical routing. Use the cable schedule, which carries routed length, cross-section and termination allowance. Routed length typically runs 1.15–1.25× the straight-line SLD distance once elevation, obstacle routing and termination loops are added.

faqs.q: Is naming the module manufacturer enough for ALMM compliance?
faqs.a: No. ALMM is enforced at model level. The BOQ must carry the exact List-I model code — "Waaree 540 W" is not a specification. Verify the model on the live MNRE portal on the day you submit, and keep a pre-approved alternative in case of delisting between bid and procurement.

faqs.q: Does ALMM List-II apply to my project?
faqs.a: It depends on bid date, commissioning date and project category. Competitively bid projects with bid submission on or before 31 August 2025 remain exempt. Net-metering and open-access projects commissioned on or before 31 December 2026 are outside List-II. PM Surya Ghar residential net metering is exempt until 31 March 2027. Behind-the-meter private captive sits outside both lists.

faqs.q: Is DCR the same as ALMM?
faqs.a: No. MNRE has confirmed the List-II orders do not change DCR provisions. A module can be listed on ALMM List-I and still fail DCR. Price DCR and non-DCR modules as separate line items — the price gap is large and it moves.

faqs.q: How much contingency should a solar BOQ carry?
faqs.a: Module and inverter quantities are exact, so they need none. On balance of system — cables, connectors, clamps and fasteners — allow 3–5% for wastage, measurement variance and site conditions. That protects margin without materially moving your bid price.

whoFor.label: Who this is for:
whoFor.body: EPC project teams, procurement managers and solar developers evaluating floating solar (FPV) projects in India — on industrial ponds, irrigation reservoirs or utility-scale water bodies under PM-SSY.

intro.p1: On 31 July 2026 the Union Cabinet approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) — a ₹5,070 crore central sector scheme to build 5,000 MW of floating solar with co-located energy storage of at least two hours, or 10,000 MWh. Projects will be sanctioned between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, with financial support disbursed up to FY 2032-33.
intro.p2: The scale is the story. India's installed floating solar base today is around 700 MW. PM-SSY targets seven times that in five years, against a NISE-assessed technical potential of roughly 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and inland water bodies. Expected investment across the programme is around ₹28,500 crore. Global floating solar deployed to date is variously estimated between 6 GW and 13 GW depending on the source — so a single national programme of 5 GW is broadly the scale of the entire world's floating fleet built so far.
intro.p3: The opportunity is large. So is the procurement complexity. Floating solar — FPV — is not ground-mount solar installed on water. The components are different, the supplier universe is far narrower, the approvals touch water resource authorities and environmental regulators alongside the CEA, and the cost premium over ground-mount is real. This guide closes the gap between ground-mount procurement experience and FPV procurement reality.

pmssyCallout.label: ⚠ The PM-SSY clause most EPC teams have missed
pmssyCallout.p1: The scheme provides up to ₹50 lakh per project as Central Financial Assistance for feasibility studies — explicitly including bathymetry and hydrography assessments and environmental studies, for the purpose of de-risking project development.
pmssyCallout.p2: Bathymetric survey data is the single input your anchoring design and pontoon BOQ cannot be finalised without. Under PM-SSY, that survey is grant-funded. Structure the work sequence to use it before you price the floating structure, not after.

floatingSolar.s1p1: Ground-mount EPC experience gives contractors a strong foundation: engineering discipline, ALMM awareness, BOQ rigour. But FPV introduces an entirely new category of components, a different structural engineering paradigm, and procurement dependencies that most Indian solar supply chains are not yet equipped to serve at scale.

groundItems: Standard DC/AC cable routing on ground
fpvItems: HDPE pontoons, anchoring systems, mooring lines
Civil work: anchoring, shore connection, cable landing
Immersion-rated DC cable and submarine AC cable
Reservoir owner + irrigation / WRD + environment + CEA + MNRE
O&M: boat access, pontoon inspection, mooring tension checks

floatingSolar.s1p2: The additional cost reflects genuine engineering complexity, not supplier margin. Pontoons must withstand UV exposure, wave action, wind loads and water-level variation across a 25-year life. Cables must be rated for continuous immersion. Anchoring must hold platforms stable through monsoon conditions and a seasonal level swing that can reach 10–20 metres. These are baseline requirements, not upgrades — they determine whether the plant survives its first monsoon.
floatingSolar.s1p3: There is an upside on the generation side that FPV bid models should capture properly: the water below the array moderates module operating temperature, which typically lifts specific yield by a low single-digit percentage against an identical ground-mount system. It is a real effect, and it is frequently overstated in vendor material — build it in at a defensible number, not at the 10–15% figure that circulates in marketing decks.
floatingSolar.s2p1: An FPV project has two procurement categories: the standard solar components where your ground-mount experience applies, and the floating-specific components where it does not. Getting the second category right is what separates successful FPV procurement from mid-project surprises.

components.spec: Virgin HDPE, UV-stabilised, density ≥940 kg/m³, buoyancy rated for module and maintenance load

components.item: Anchoring system (concrete dead weights / helix anchors / shore anchors)
components.spec: Site-specific: water depth, bed composition, seasonal level variation, wind fetch
High Modulus Polyethylene, UV rated, break load and creep specified, tension monitoring provision
IP68 junction box, PID resistance (IEC TS 62804), high humidity and salt-mist resistance where applicable (IEC 61701)
Tinned copper, XLPO insulation, 1.5 kV DC, rated for continuous immersion (AD8 duty) — EN 50618 / IEC 62930, not IEC 60227
Armoured submarine cable to IEC 63026 or IEC 60502-2, suitable for reservoir bed routing, with cable-landing transition joints
IP65/IP66, corrosion-resistant enclosure, humidity-rated; floating platform or shore-mounted, decided at design stage
IP67 minimum, marine-grade stainless hardware, drip loops at every entry
Minimum 2-hour duration; LFP racks, PCS, EMS/BMS, HVAC, fire detection and suppression, shore-side civil and containerisation
Anti-slip, load-rated for maintenance crew and tools, gangway to shore, handrails
Transformer, HT panel, metering cubicle, cable landing structure, earthing mat on shore

components.item: O&M boat and marine access equipment
components.spec: Motorised dinghy or inflatable, life jackets, and a documented water-safety protocol

floatingSolar.essNote: Note the ESS row. PM-SSY makes co-located storage mandatory at a minimum of two hours. Any FPV BOQ prepared for a PM-SSY project that treats storage as a later decision is incomplete from day one.

hdpeCallout.label: ⚠ Key procurement warning
hdpeCallout.title: Virgin vs recycled HDPE — the difference that determines project life
items: Virgin HDPE, UV-stabilised, density ≥940 kg/m³, lasts 25+ years on water without degrading, cracking or losing buoyancy under continuous UV and temperature cycling.

Recycled-content pontoons — often 15–25% cheaper — can show surface degradation within 5–7 years on water. Mid-project replacement costs a large multiple of the initial saving, and it happens while the plant is generating.

Verify with a test package, not a single certificate. Melt flow rate to ISO 1133 and density to ISO 1183 tell you about the resin grade; they do not by themselves prove virgin material. Ask additionally for resin supplier batch certificates, carbon black / UV stabiliser content (ISO 6964 or ASTM D1603), oxidative induction time (ISO 11357-6), and an accelerated weathering report (ISO 4892 or ASTM G154).
Rule of thumb: if a pontoon supplier cannot produce virgin HDPE traceability to resin batch level, do not proceed — regardless of price.

floatingSolar.s3p1: The premium of floating over ground-mount is real, and knowing where it lives tells procurement where to optimise and where to accept it. The table below is built bottom-up: the component rows sum to the totals.

costRows.driver: IP68 junction box, anti-corrosion and humidity specification
Higher IP rating, marine-grade enclosures, platform mounting
HDPE floats, anchoring and mooring — no standardised domestic supply chain
Immersion-rated DC and submarine AC grades, largely imported
Underwater anchoring, cable landing, shore connection infrastructure
Marine logistics, specialist installation crew, boat access, narrower window

costTotal.driver: ≈40–65% premium, concentrated in structure, cable and execution

floatingSolar.s3p2: Read this table with three caveats. (1) Module rates are non-DCR. Where DCR applies, add roughly ₹6–9/Wp — JMK Research put domestic non-DCR TOPCon at ₹14.2/Wp against DCR TOPCon at ₹22.3/Wp in April 2026, with DCR then rising 9.4% month-on-month in May. (2) Energy storage sits outside this ₹/Wp and is priced separately on a ₹/kWh basis; under PM-SSY the ₹1 crore per MW CFA offsets 15–25% of the combined cost. (3) As a real benchmark: NTPC's 100 MW Ramagundam plant was built for ₹423 crore — about ₹42/Wp on AC capacity, or roughly ₹29/Wp on its 145 MW DC, at 2019–2022 prices.
floatingSolar.s3p3: Roughly 60% of the total differential sits in the floating structure and cable categories — which is also where Indian domestic supply is weakest. The strategic decision for most EPC contractors is whether to source pontoons and submarine cable from the small Indian manufacturing base or import them. Imports can run 15–25% cheaper ex-works but carry 8–12 week lead times, container freight in the region of USD 800–1,200 per container to port, and customs clearance on top.

midCta.title: Procuring solar equipment for a floating project?
midCta.desc: Headsup B2B connects EPC teams to verified suppliers of ALMM-compliant modules, marine-grade cables and FPV-spec electrical equipment — with pan-India delivery and 60-day procurement credit.

pullQuote.text: The pontoon and mooring system is where floating solar projects succeed or fail — not the panels. A ₹2/Wp saving on modules means nothing if your platform needs replacing in year seven because someone substituted recycled HDPE to win the bid.

challenges.title: A narrow domestic supplier base for FPV components
challenges.body: India has only a handful of domestic HDPE pontoon manufacturers with a commissioned FPV track record. For projects above 10 MW, supply capacity becomes a lead-time risk — and PM-SSY will pull that capacity in several directions at once.
challenges.action: Pre-qualify suppliers before tender award, not after

challenges.title: Multi-agency clearances with overlapping timelines
challenges.body: Permission comes from the reservoir owner first — a state water resources or irrigation department, or a PSU for its own reservoir — then the pollution control board or MoEFCC where the water body triggers it, and the CEA and DISCOM for connectivity. The Central Water Commission's role is technical and advisory on dam safety rather than a project clearance.
challenges.action: Map the clearance chain before finalising the BOQ and procurement schedule

challenges.title: The installation window is narrow
challenges.body: On-water work on a live reservoir is weather-dependent, and the monsoon (June–September) generally halts it entirely. Missing the pre-monsoon window costs four to five months, with the financing and penalty consequences that follow.
challenges.action: Complete procurement by March–April for pre-monsoon commissioning

challenges.title: Submarine cable import lead times
challenges.body: Submarine AC cable and immersion-rated floating DC cable of FPV specification are largely imported. Lead times of 10–14 weeks are standard and customs clearance adds two to three more. Late cable procurement kills the installation window.
challenges.action: Order submarine cable at project sanction — not at EPC mobilisation

challenges.title: ALMM and FPV specification are two separate tests
challenges.body: Modules for government FPV projects must be on ALMM List-I and meet FPV requirements — IP68 junction box, PID resistance, humidity performance — and, depending on bid and commissioning dates, ALMM List-II cell sourcing as well. Not every List-I model qualifies for water deployment.
challenges.action: Verify FPV suitability and ALMM status as two independent checks

challenges.title: Water level variation drives anchoring design
challenges.body: Reservoir levels can vary 10–20 metres seasonally, and anchoring — dead weights, helix anchors or shoreline points — depends entirely on site-specific bathymetric and bed-composition data. Pontoon and mooring quantities cannot be finalised without it.
challenges.action: Commission the bathymetric survey first — PM-SSY funds it up to ₹50 lakh

omkareshwarCallout.label: ⚠ Learn from Omkareshwar
omkareshwarCallout.body: India's largest floating solar park at Omkareshwar in Madhya Pradesh suffered storm damage in April 2024, reportedly attributed to inadequate anchoring. It is the clearest available demonstration of the point this guide keeps returning to: on water, the mooring and anchoring package — not the module — is the component that decides whether the asset survives. Price it, engineer it site-specifically, and do not accept a generic anchoring design carried over from another reservoir.

floatingSolar.s5p1: Supplier selection for FPV is fundamentally different from ground-mount procurement. Three quotes and lowest compliant bid is not a sufficient method when what you are buying is a floating structure that must survive 25 years on a water body you do not control.

criteria.item: Installed FPV track record in India
criteria.verify: Minimum three commissioned projects above 1 MW; demand a site visit or commissioning documents. Must have.
MFR (ISO 1133), density (ISO 1183), UV stabiliser content, OIT and accelerated weathering report, plus resin batch certificates. Must have.

criteria.item: Production capacity vs your peak demand
criteria.verify: Monthly output against your delivery schedule. Ask specifically how they intend to serve PM-SSY volumes without displacing you.
In-house structural or marine engineering for site-specific design, or a demonstrated third-party partnership. Ask to see a completed anchoring calculation.
Service presence within reasonable reach of site; pontoon repair and replacement track record; spares availability commitment.

criteria.item: Total landed cost and payment terms
criteria.verify: Landed at site, not ex-works — include freight, insurance and duties. Import duty on Chinese floats typically adds 8–15%.

suppliers.label: Indian FPV technology and float suppliers to consider
items: Ciel & Terre India — French FPV technology company with an Indian subsidiary; proprietary Hydrelio floating system; a long international track record across 30+ countries.
Prabhdayal and Adtech — supplied the floaters and anchoring system for NTPC's 100 MW Ramagundam plant, India's largest completed FPV project.
Floatex Solar — India-based float and FPV systems supplier with ferrocement and HDPE float technologies and a domestic manufacturing footprint.

Domestic HDPE float and mooring hardware manufacturers — a small group of Indian fabricators now competing with imports on landed cost, several of them ISO 9001 certified and offering customisation for 400–630 Wp module formats.
Large integrated EPC firms — BHEL, Tata Power Solar, L&T and Sterling & Wilson have executed utility-scale FPV in India and bring integrated float sourcing to projects at that scale.
suppliers.note: Supplier capabilities and capacity claims change quickly in this segment. Treat this as a starting shortlist and verify track record, certification and current production capacity directly before pre-qualification.

steps.title: Commission the bathymetric and geotechnical survey before any procurement
steps.body: Water depth, seasonal level variation, bed composition (rock, silt, clay) and wind and wave data are all needed before you can design anchoring and finalise the pontoon platform specification. Under PM-SSY this survey attracts CFA of up to ₹50 lakh per project — use it. Procuring without this data means a BOQ that will be revised after mobilisation, when revisions are expensive.

steps.title: Start clearances at sanction, not after engineering
steps.body: Reservoir-owner permission, state irrigation or water resources approval and environmental clearance can each take two to six months and they do not run neatly in parallel. Pontoons delivered to a site without clearance mean storage cost, damage risk and idle capital.

steps.title: Order submarine and floating cable first
steps.body: These are the longest lead-time items in the project. Place the order within about two weeks of financial close. Every week lost here compresses the installation window and pushes you closer to monsoon.

steps.title: Run the ALMM and FPV-suitability checks together, at order stage
steps.body: Cross-reference shortlisted modules against ALMM List-I, your List-II obligation for the project category, and the FPV technical requirements. IP68 junction box, PID certification and humidity specification must be confirmed on the product datasheet and test report — not on the marketing sheet.

steps.title: Schedule pontoon delivery to the installation window, not to project start
steps.body: HDPE pontoons are bulky and need covered, dry storage. Deliver three to four weeks before on-water installation begins, and coordinate with your marine logistics contractor on site access and unloading infrastructure at the water's edge.

steps.title: Procure the storage system on its own track
steps.body: Under PM-SSY the ESS is not optional. Battery racks, PCS, EMS, HVAC and fire safety carry their own lead times, their own certification requirements and their own shore-side civil scope. Running it as an afterthought to the PV package is how commissioning dates slip.

steps.title: Build a dedicated FPV O&M plan into the project BOQ
steps.body: FPV O&M is not ground-mount O&M. Annual cost includes boat charter or ownership, pontoon inspection, underwater cable inspection, mooring tension checks, bird fouling and algal growth management, and cleaning with restricted access. Price these into the BOQ rather than discovering them after commissioning.

caseStudy.label: Ramagundam 100 MW — what procurement actually looked like
caseStudy.p1: NTPC's Ramagundam floating solar project in Telangana remains India's largest completed FPV plant. It was executed by BHEL under an EPC contract awarded in June 2019, and the final 20 MW was declared under commercial operation on 1 July 2022 — roughly three years from award to full commissioning, not the compressed timeline often quoted.

facts.v: HMPE rope to 9-tonne pre-cast dead weights

caseStudy.p2: Each block carries its own floating platform with inverter, transformer and HT breaker — an all-floating electrical configuration that is worth studying before you decide whether to put your own power conversion on water or on shore. The three-year timeline reflects exactly what this guide warns about: multi-agency clearances, monsoon-constrained installation windows, and the absence of an established domestic FPV supply chain at 100 MW scale.
caseStudy.attribution: — NTPC and Ministry of Power public disclosures, 2019–2022

takeaways.title: FPV is not ground-mount on water — it is a different procurement discipline.
takeaways.body: Pontoons, anchoring, mooring and submarine cable require supplier relationships and technical verification that ground-mount experience does not prepare you for.

takeaways.title: The 40–65% cost premium is concentrated in structure, cable and execution.
takeaways.body: Modules and inverters are only modestly more expensive. About 60% of the differential sits in the float and cable categories, which is precisely where Indian supply is thinnest.

takeaways.title: Virgin HDPE traceability is non-negotiable.
takeaways.body: The difference between a 25-year pontoon and a seven-year pontoon is raw material quality. Get the MFR and density tests, the UV stabiliser content, the OIT result and the resin batch certificates before you sign a supply agreement.

takeaways.title: Submarine cable and clearances have the longest lead times.
takeaways.body: Start both on the day of financial close. Every week of delay compresses a monsoon-constrained installation window that will not stretch to accommodate you.

takeaways.title: Use the PM-SSY structure deliberately.
takeaways.body: ₹1 crore per MW after commissioning, up to ₹50 lakh for feasibility including bathymetry, and a mandatory two-hour storage obligation are all design inputs, not footnotes. Build the survey grant into your sequence and the ESS into your BOQ from the first draft.

takeaways.title: PM-SSY creates an opportunity and a bottleneck simultaneously.
takeaways.body: As 5,000 MW of FPV procurement enters the pipeline against a domestic base of roughly 700 MW, pontoon and cable suppliers will face capacity pressure. Early pre-qualification and framework agreements will be a genuine competitive advantage through 2026–27.

faqs.q: How much more does floating solar cost than ground-mount in India?
faqs.a: Turnkey FPV runs ₹43–65/Wp against ₹30–40/Wp for ground-mount — a premium of roughly 40–65%. About 60% of that differential sits in the pontoon and cable categories. Energy storage is priced separately on a ₹/kWh basis, and under PM-SSY the ₹1 crore per MW CFA offsets 15–25% of the combined cost.

faqs.q: What does PM-SSY actually fund?
faqs.a: ₹5,070 crore for 5,000 MW of floating solar with 10,000 MWh of co-located storage. Central Financial Assistance is ₹1 crore per MW after successful commissioning, plus up to ₹50 lakh per project for feasibility studies — explicitly including bathymetry, hydrography and environmental assessments. Sanctions run FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, with disbursement to FY 2032-33.

faqs.q: Why does the bathymetric survey have to come first?
faqs.a: Water depth, seasonal level variation, bed composition and wind and wave data determine the anchoring design, and the anchoring design determines pontoon and mooring quantities. Without the survey your BOQ is an estimate that will be revised after mobilisation — when revisions are expensive. Under PM-SSY the survey is grant-funded, so there is no cost argument for skipping it.

faqs.q: How do I verify that pontoons are virgin HDPE?
faqs.a: Ask for a test package, not a single certificate. Melt flow rate (ISO 1133) and density (ISO 1183) describe the resin grade but do not prove virgin material on their own. Add resin supplier batch certificates, carbon black / UV stabiliser content (ISO 6964 or ASTM D1603), oxidative induction time (ISO 11357-6) and an accelerated weathering report (ISO 4892 or ASTM G154). If a supplier cannot trace to resin batch level, do not proceed regardless of price.

faqs.q: Does an ALMM List-I module automatically work for floating solar?
faqs.a: No. ALMM listing and FPV suitability are two independent checks. An FPV module additionally needs an IP68 junction box, PID resistance to IEC TS 62804, and high-humidity and salt-mist performance where the site requires it. Confirm all of it on the product datasheet and test report, not the marketing sheet.

faqs.q: When should procurement be completed for a monsoon-constrained site?
faqs.a: Complete procurement by March–April so on-water installation finishes before the June–September monsoon. Submarine cable carries 10–14 week lead times plus two to three weeks of customs, so it should be ordered within about two weeks of financial close. Missing the pre-monsoon window costs four to five months.

faqs.q: Does floating solar actually generate more than ground-mount?
faqs.a: Yes, but modestly. The water below the array moderates module operating temperature, typically lifting specific yield by a low single-digit percentage against an identical ground-mount system. The 10–15% figures that circulate in vendor decks are not defensible — model the gain at a conservative number.

marketAlert.label: ⚠ Market alert — August 2026
marketAlert.body: Wood Mackenzie forecasts utility-scale solar system costs will rise 20% by Q4 2026 as ALMM-II cell capacity constraints tighten. EPC contractors who bid on H2 2026 projects at pre-June pricing face direct margin exposure. This article gives you the data and the playbook.

whoFor.label: Who this is for:
whoFor.body: EPC project managers, procurement heads, and bid teams at solar contracting firms managing active projects or preparing bids for H2 2026 and FY 2026-27 tenders.

intro.p1: India's solar market in 2026 is a study in contradictions. Installation volumes are at an all-time high — 34 GWdc added in H1 2026 alone, 38% above H1 2025 levels. The pipeline is enormous. And yet, for EPC contractors on the ground, margin pressure has never been more acute.
intro.p2: The reason is ALMM-II — the MNRE mandate that came into force in June 2026, requiring solar modules used in government-supported projects to be manufactured from domestically produced cells. The policy is strategically sound. The near-term supply chain reality is brutal. India's domestic cell capacity stood at roughly 88 GW in 2026 against annual module demand trending toward 50 GW — but utilisation rates remain insufficient, and Wood Mackenzie forecasts system prices rising 20% by Q4 2026 as cell availability tightens.
intro.p3: For contractors who won tenders in Q4 2025 or Q1 2026 at pre-ALMM-II module prices, this is not a future risk. It is a present reality that is already compressing margins on active projects. This guide gives you the complete picture — what is driving prices, what the numbers actually look like today, and the margin protection strategies that experienced procurement teams are using right now.

solarModulePrices.s1p1: Module pricing in India has two distinct tracks in 2026: ALMM-I compliant modules (the broader list, covering finished modules), and the narrower universe of ALMM-II compliant modules (modules made with domestically manufactured cells, mandatory for government projects from June 2026). The price gap between these two categories is now a hard procurement reality.
solarModulePrices.priceNote: Note: Module prices vary significantly by project size, supplier, location, and payment terms. The relative price positioning below reflects broad industry trends as of August 2026 — always get current quotes from verified suppliers before finalising your BOQ.

almmCallout.label: ⚠ Critical pricing context — August 2026
almmCallout.title: The ALMM-II price gap is now the defining procurement variable
items: ALMM-II mandatory from June 1, 2026 for all government-funded projects — SECI, NTPC, state DISCOM, PM-KUSUM, PM Surya Ghar
ALMM-II exemption extended to December 31, 2026 for net metering and open access projects only
MNRE waived ALMM-II for projects nearing completion that submitted applications by July 23, 2026 — if you missed this window, full compliance applies

India's certified domestic cell capacity is a fraction of total module production capacity — meaning the compliant supply pool is structurally small relative to demand, creating upward price pressure on ALMM-II modules
Anti-dumping duties of up to 30% on Chinese-origin solar products were recommended by DGTR in September 2025 — final notification still pending but adds further cost uncertainty

solarModulePrices.s2p1: The price picture for solar modules in India in 2026 is the result of two opposing forces — upward pressure from domestic policy and compliance requirements, and downward pressure from a globally oversupplied module market. Understanding both helps procurement teams identify where they have room to manoeuvre.

drivers.label: ↑ Pushing prices up
drivers.title: ALMM-II domestic cell mandate
drivers.body: Modules for government projects must now use domestically manufactured cells. India's cell capacity is far below module capacity — this supply-demand mismatch drives a ₹8–10/Wp compliance premium.
drivers.impact: Meaningful price premium on ALMM-II compliant modules vs. non-DCR

drivers.label: ↑ Pushing prices up
drivers.title: 20% Basic Customs Duty on imported cells
drivers.body: Chinese solar cells at USD 0.042/Wp rise to USD 0.053/Wp after 20% BCD and 7.5% AIDC — adding ₹0.93/Wp landed cost even before module assembly margins.
drivers.impact: Significant landed cost addition on imported cell-based modules

drivers.label: ↑ Pushing prices up
drivers.title: Rush demand in H1 2026 depleted inventory
drivers.body: 34 GW installed in H1 2026 as developers raced to commission before ALMM-II — depleting compliant module inventory across all major manufacturers. Lead times stretched to 10–14 weeks for DCR product.

drivers.label: ↑ Pushing prices up
drivers.title: ISTS charge waivers reducing — adding project cost
drivers.body: Inter-state transmission charge waivers fell from 75% to 50% for projects commissioned from July 2026. Full phase-out by July 2028. This adds to total project cost, squeezing overall EPC economics even where module prices hold.
drivers.impact: Additional project cost burden — varies by project location and capacity

drivers.label: ↓ Holding prices down
drivers.title: Global module manufacturing oversupply
drivers.body: Global module manufacturing capacity exceeds 1,100 GW against ~650 GW of installation demand in 2026. China's massive overcapacity keeps ex-factory module prices near historic lows at USD 0.085–0.15/Wp.
drivers.impact: Private project module costs remain suppressed

drivers.label: ↓ Holding prices down
drivers.title: Competitive EPC bidding keeps contractor pressure high
drivers.body: India's EPC market remains intensely competitive. Developers routinely push for lower tariffs, squeezing EPC margins even as procurement costs rise. This limits how much cost increase contractors can pass through in negotiations.
drivers.impact: Absorption pressure remains on EPC firms

solarModulePrices.s3p1: Since modules typically account for nearly half of total EPC project cost, even a moderate increase in procurement price creates a significant gap between what was priced at bid stage and what must be paid today. Every contractor's situation is different — project size, contract terms, payment schedules, and supplier agreements all affect the actual impact. But the direction is clear: procurement costs are higher now than they were at the time most H1 2026 bids were submitted, and that gap needs active management.

strategies.title: Lock in ALMM-II module pricing now — before Q4 tightening
strategies.body: Wood Mackenzie forecasts the steepest price increases in Q3–Q4 2026 as cell capacity constraints peak. Contractors with active or upcoming projects should place forward purchase orders for ALMM-II compliant modules now — even for projects commissioning in Q1 2027. Price lock-ins with confirmed delivery schedules protect against Q4 spot market premiums.
strategies.impact: ↗ Forward orders typically offer better pricing than spot Q4 procurement

strategies.title: Separate module procurement from EPC bid pricing — use escalation clauses
strategies.body: For new tenders, negotiate procurement price escalation clauses tied to MNRE-notified indices or published spot module prices. A 3–5% escalation provision for module costs protects you from the kind of 15–25% price movement seen in H1 2026 without requiring you to overbid on base rates and lose tenders.
strategies.impact: ↗ Shifts a meaningful portion of price risk to the developer contractually

strategies.title: Evaluate non-DCR modules for open access and private C&I projects
strategies.body: ALMM-II is mandatory only for government-funded projects. For open access, captive, and C&I solar — where developers are private — non-DCR modules remain fully eligible and carry a materially lower price than DCR-compliant equivalents. Deliberately segmenting your project portfolio between DCR-mandatory and DCR-optional projects optimises your blended procurement cost.
strategies.impact: ↗ Non-DCR modules are materially cheaper — significant saving on qualifying projects

strategies.title: Build a 3-supplier shortlist for ALMM-II compliant modules
strategies.body: Single-supplier dependency for DCR modules is a critical risk when supply is constrained. Qualify at least 3 ALMM-II listed manufacturers (Waaree, Vikram Solar, Adani Solar, Premier Energies, Tata Power Solar are current major List-II certified manufacturers) and maintain framework agreements with at least 2. Backup qualification takes 2–3 weeks; do it now, not mid-project.

strategies.title: Use procurement credit to time purchases at price dips
strategies.body: Module prices are not uniformly high — they dip when developer rush periods end and supply catches up temporarily. A pre-approved procurement credit facility allows you to act immediately when a price dip window opens, rather than waiting for internal financial approvals or working capital availability. The cost of 45-day credit is invariably less than a 3% price premium avoided.
strategies.impact: ↗ Buy at dips, not at peaks — credit as timing tool

strategies.title: Re-examine BOQ line items for BoS cost offsets
strategies.body: When module costs rise, review the full BOQ for BoS components where market prices have fallen. DC cables, mounting structures, and inverters are all subject to different price dynamics. A structured BOQ review often finds ₹10–20L of cost offset that partially compensates for module price increases without quality compromise.
strategies.impact: ↗ Recover ₹10–20L per project from BoS optimisation

outlook.title: Peak price pressure — tightest ALMM-II supply window
outlook.body: Post-H1 rush depletion + ALMM-II compliance in full effect + no new cell capacity commissioned yet. Worst pricing environment for DCR module procurement. Avoid spot buying if possible.

outlook.title: Partial stabilisation — new cell capacity begins coming online
outlook.body: Waaree, Premier Energies and Adani Solar cell expansion capacity enters production. ALMM-II exemption for open access expires December 31. Some price relief on DCR modules expected but limited.

outlook.title: Meaningful price stabilisation begins
outlook.body: Additional cell capacity from PLI-backed manufacturers reduces supply squeeze. DCR module premiums expected to moderate from current peaks. Better procurement environment for projects tendering now.

outlook.title: Full price stabilisation — per Wood Mackenzie forecast
outlook.body: Wood Mackenzie predicts prices stabilise by 2029 as more cell capacity becomes operational — contingent on consistent policy and timely manufacturer execution. 130 GW of additional cell capacity is slated to come online by 2029.

avoid.label: What to avoid in the current market
avoid.title: High-risk procurement behaviours in an ALMM-II constrained market
items: Spot procurement for large volumes — spot prices in Aug–Sep 2026 carry the highest premiums; forward orders with framework suppliers are significantly cheaper

takeaways.title: Solar module prices for ALMM-II compliant product are up 15–25% since January 2026.
takeaways.body: Wood Mackenzie forecasts further 20% system cost increases by Q4 2026. This is not a temporary blip; it reflects a structural supply constraint that persists until 2028–29.

takeaways.title: The ALMM-II compliance premium is now ₹8–10/Wp.
takeaways.body: On a 10 MW project, that is ₹80–100 lakh of additional cost versus non-DCR modules. For contractors who bid at pre-June rates, this directly hits active project margins.

takeaways.title: Private C&I and open access projects have an important cost advantage through December 2026.
takeaways.body: ALMM-II exemption for these segments means non-DCR modules are still eligible — at ₹22–26/Wp vs ₹32–40/Wp for DCR product. Portfolio segmentation is a real cost optimisation lever.

takeaways.title: Forward purchasing and price-lock agreements are the most effective near-term protection.
takeaways.body: Spot procurement at Q3–Q4 2026 ALMM-II module prices is the highest-cost scenario. Framework supplier agreements and forward orders are the procurement standard for any EPC firm bidding on H2 2026 or FY27 projects.

takeaways.title: Prices will stabilise — but not until 2028–29.
takeaways.body: Any contractor building a multi-year project pipeline should factor elevated DCR module pricing into bid models for at least the next 6–8 quarters.

faqs.q: How much have solar module prices risen in India in 2026?
faqs.a: ALMM-II compliant (DCR) module prices are up roughly 15–25% since January 2026, and Wood Mackenzie forecasts a further 20% rise in utility-scale system costs by Q4 2026. Non-DCR modules have been broadly stable or softening, because global manufacturing capacity (1,100+ GW) far exceeds 2026 installation demand (~650 GW).

faqs.q: What exactly is the ALMM-II premium?
faqs.a: Roughly ₹8–10/Wp over comparable non-DCR modules — about ₹80–100 lakh on a 10 MW project. It exists because ALMM-II requires domestically manufactured cells, and India's certified cell capacity is small relative to module demand.

faqs.q: Does ALMM-II apply to my project?
faqs.a: It is mandatory from 1 June 2026 for all government-funded projects — SECI, NTPC, state DISCOM, PM-KUSUM and PM Surya Ghar. Net metering and open access projects are exempt until 31 December 2026. Private C&I, captive and open access projects can still use non-DCR modules, which are materially cheaper.

faqs.q: I bid this project before June 2026. What are my options now?
faqs.a: Four levers, in order of impact: place forward orders to avoid Q3–Q4 spot premiums; check whether any part of your portfolio qualifies as non-DCR; review the BOQ for BoS cost offsets (₹10–20L is commonly recoverable); and use procurement credit to buy into price dips rather than at peaks. For anything not yet contracted, add an escalation clause.

faqs.q: Is an ALMM-I certificate enough for a government project?
faqs.a: No. ALMM-I and ALMM-II are separate lists. ALMM-I covers finished modules; ALMM-II additionally requires domestically manufactured cells. For government projects after June 2026, ALMM-I alone is not sufficient — verify List-II certification specifically.

faqs.q: When will module prices come back down?
faqs.a: Partial relief is expected from Q4 2026 as Waaree, Premier Energies and Adani Solar cell expansions enter production, with meaningful stabilisation in Q1–Q2 2027. Wood Mackenzie expects full stabilisation only by 2029, when around 130 GW of additional cell capacity is slated to be operational.

faqs.q: Should I buy modules on the spot market right now?
faqs.a: Aug–Sep 2026 is the worst window — post-rush inventory depletion, full ALMM-II enforcement, and no new cell capacity yet. Spot prices carry the highest premiums. Forward orders with framework suppliers are significantly cheaper for anything above small volumes.

whoFor.label: Who this is for:
whoFor.body: Solar EPC contractors, sub-contractors, and project developers managing working capital across concurrent projects in India.

intro.p1: India added a record 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025–26, crossing 150 GW of cumulative installed solar by 31 March 2026 — and the pipeline ahead is larger still. For EPC contractors, the opportunity has never been bigger. The constraint is almost never technical. It is financial.
intro.p2: The structural reality of solar EPC economics is this: you procure equipment weeks before milestone payments arrive. On a 5 MW project, that gap can mean ₹3–5 crore of your own money sitting in modules and cables on a project site while you wait for a developer's payment cycle to turn. Multiply that across two or three concurrent projects and you have a working capital hole that limits how aggressively you can bid — and how fast you can grow.

solarFinancing.s1p1: Solar EPC payment structures are milestone-based — typically tied to mobilisation, civil completion, equipment installation, and commissioning. The problem is that equipment procurement must happen upfront, often 8–12 weeks before the installation milestone that triggers the corresponding payment.

gapCard.label: The cash flow gap — how it actually works
gapCard.title: A 5 MW project, won at ₹4 crore/MW = ₹20 crore contract

rows.v: Modules, inverters, cables procured = ₹8–9 crore spend.

gapCard.note: That is a 10–14 week window in which roughly ₹6.5 crore of net procurement outflow is funded entirely by your own working capital. Run three concurrent projects and the exposure compounds to ₹15–20 crore.

solarFinancing.s1p2: Working capital requirements for MW-scale solar EPC contracts typically run ₹2–20 crore — and that is before EMD/bid security, which adds another ₹5–50 lakh per tender depending on project scale. For a mid-size contractor running an active order book of 30–50 MW, the aggregate working capital exposure is substantial.
solarFinancing.s2p1: The working capital constraint operates on two levels. The first is visible: you simply cannot fund the procurement on a new project while existing projects are still in their payment cycle. The second is less visible but more damaging: you overbid — padding your price to create a liquidity buffer — and lose tenders to competitors who have already solved the financing problem.
solarFinancing.s2p2: The pattern is well documented in the market. Odyssey Energy Solutions has publicly reported enabling a leading Indian solar EPC contractor to execute close to 200 MW of projects through a ₹32 crore procurement-linked credit facility, ensuring timely equipment sourcing while preserving the contractor's own working capital. That contractor's order book was already around ₹1,100 crore. The constraint was not technical capability or market access. It was working capital.

pullQuote.text: The contractors consistently winning on solar execution have solved the financing problem first. They bid aggressively because they can fund procurement without waiting for milestone receipts.

solarFinancing.s6p1: Procurement-linked credit is different from a general working capital loan. Instead of a disbursement into your bank account, the credit is activated at the point of order — your supplier is paid, you receive the goods, and you repay within the agreed window (30, 45, or 60 days). No separate loan application, no collateral pledge, no processing delays.

steps.title: Onboard and get a credit limit pre-approved
steps.body: Submit GST returns, 2 years ITR, and 6 months bank statements. Assessment focuses on cash flows and order history — not fixed asset collateral. Approval typically within 2–5 working days.

steps.title: Place your equipment order and select credit payment
steps.body: Choose 30, 45, or 60-day repayment at checkout. The credit is activated immediately — your supplier is paid on time, and your procurement schedule is not delayed waiting for your own cash.

steps.title: Equipment delivered, project progresses
steps.body: Modules, inverters, and BoS arrive on schedule. Your project milestones proceed — civil work, installation, commissioning — while the credit clock runs in parallel with your payment cycle.

steps.title: Repay when your milestone payment arrives
steps.body: When your developer's payment clears, you repay the procurement credit. Cash flow aligned — you pay for equipment with the money the project generates, not from your working capital reserve.

steps.title: Credit limit grows with your transaction history
steps.body: Consistent repayment builds your platform credit profile. Higher limits unlock over time — enabling larger projects and more concurrent workstreams without proportionally increasing capital deployment.

qualify.label: Qualification criteria — procurement credit
qualify.title: What you need to get approved quickly
items: GST registration + 12 months returns: a clean GST filing history is the primary signal of business legitimacy and revenue.
Last 2 years ITR (business entity): profitability matters less than revenue consistency — even breakeven businesses qualify.
6 months primary bank statements: average monthly balance and inflow patterns determine your initial credit limit.
Project order / LOI: a purchase order or Letter of Intent from your client validates procurement intent and helps justify the limit.
No collateral required: unlike a bank OD, procurement credit is assessed on business cash flows — no property or equipment pledge needed.

limitRows.profile: New EPC firm (1–3 years, ₹50 L – ₹2 Cr turnover)

winWays.label: 5 ways credit helps you win more bids
winWays.title: Beyond just plugging the cash flow gap
items: Bid without a liquidity buffer in your price: contractors who self-fund procurement build a 3–5% risk premium into bids. Remove that and you bid more competitively.
Commit to suppliers faster: with credit pre-approved, you issue POs within hours of winning a tender — before competitors have even arranged funding.
Lock in current module prices: procurement credit lets you place forward orders when prices are favourable — not when your cash flow permits.
Run more concurrent projects: your working capital constraint becomes your credit limit rather than your bank balance, materially multiplying the projects one rupee of own capital can support.
Build supplier priority: on-time payment via credit earns you priority supplier status — critical when ALMM-II compliant module supply is tight.

takeaways.title: The working capital gap in solar EPC is structural.
takeaways.body: Procurement happens 8–12 weeks before milestone payments. Every contractor faces it; the ones who solve it win more bids.

takeaways.title: The cost of procurement credit is a fraction of the price competitiveness you give up by padding a bid for liquidity.
takeaways.body: Model your own numbers before deciding.

takeaways.title: 60-day procurement credit is the right window for most EPC payment cycles.
takeaways.body: It aligns repayment with installation milestone receipts without excessive cost.

takeaways.title: Collateral-free procurement credit is accessible to contractors with 1+ years of GST filing history and a project order in hand.
takeaways.body: No property pledge required.

takeaways.title: Credit limits scale with transaction history.
takeaways.body: Starting with smaller orders and repaying on time builds the profile that unlocks larger limits for bigger projects.

takeaways.title: In a tight ALMM-II module supply market, on-time payment via credit earns supplier priority.
takeaways.body: That is an advantage money alone cannot buy later.

faqs.q: What is the typical working capital requirement for a 5 MW solar EPC project?
faqs.a: On a ₹4 crore/MW contract value with standard payment milestones, a 5 MW project typically needs ₹6–8 crore of working capital to bridge the gap between equipment procurement (weeks 4–8) and the installation milestone payment (weeks 14–18). This varies with the contract payment schedule and your procurement timing.

faqs.q: Is collateral required for procurement credit for solar EPC?
faqs.a: Platform-linked procurement credit does not require property or equipment collateral. Assessment is based on GST returns, ITR, bank statements, and order history. Traditional bank overdrafts and IREDA loans do require security — typically fixed assets or project receivables.

faqs.q: How quickly can procurement credit be activated for a new order?
faqs.a: Once onboarded with a pre-approved limit, procurement credit is activated at the point of order — typically the same day. Initial onboarding and credit assessment takes 2–5 working days from document submission.

faqs.q: What is the EMD/bid security requirement for solar EPC tenders in 2026?
faqs.a: EMD ranges from ₹1–3 lakh for small rooftop tenders to ₹1–5 crore for large utility-scale bids. MSME-registered contractors are exempt in many tenders. EMD is separate from working capital — it is typically a bank guarantee or demand draft, released after award or rejection.

faqs.q: Can I use IREDA financing for procurement working capital?
faqs.a: IREDA had its strongest year yet in FY 2025–26 — record sanctions of ₹51,883 crore (up 9% year on year) and disbursements of ₹34,946 crore, with the loan book growing 22% to ₹93,075 crore. But IREDA is primarily a project finance lender for commissioned and under-construction assets, not a working capital solution for EPC contractors mid-execution. For procurement gaps, platform credit or NBFC facilities are faster and better suited.

faqs.q: Does taking procurement credit affect my company's CIBIL score?
faqs.a: Procurement credit used responsibly and repaid on time builds your business credit profile and CIBIL MSME rank. Late repayment will affect it negatively. Consistent on-time repayment is also what unlocks higher limits over time.

whoFor.label: Who this is for:
whoFor.body: Solar EPC contractors, project developers, and procurement teams evaluating the green hydrogen opportunity and its implications for solar project pipelines in India.

intro.p1: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission launched in January 2023 with a total outlay of ₹19,744 crore, targeting 5 million metric tonnes per annum (MMTPA) of domestic green hydrogen production by 2030 — alongside roughly 125 GW of associated renewable energy capacity. That renewable capacity has to be built. By somebody.
intro.p2: For solar EPC contractors, green hydrogen is not a distant market. SIGHT Tranche-1 plants begin commercial operation from August 2026 — meaning the renewable plants that power these electrolysers are moving from tender to procurement now. The contractors who understand this connection, and who can source and deliver dedicated renewable infrastructure at the scale these projects demand, are positioning for what could become India's largest new solar tender category of the next five years.
intro.p3: This guide explains the green hydrogen value chain, what the solar procurement opportunity actually looks like today, and what EPC contractors should do to be ready for it.

greenHydrogen.s1p1: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using an electrolyser powered entirely by renewable energy. No fossil fuels, no process carbon emissions. The hydrogen produced is used as an industrial feedstock (fertilisers, refineries, steel), as a fuel for heavy transport, or exported as green ammonia.

chain.title: Solar Plant
chain.body: Dedicated RE source — typically 4–6× the electrolyser MW capacity

chain.title: Electrolyser
chain.body: Splits water into H₂ and O₂ using renewable electricity

chain.title: Green Hydrogen
chain.body: Used in fertilisers, refining, steel — or exported as ammonia

chain.title: End Use
chain.body: Industry, transport, export — reducing fossil fuel dependence

greenHydrogen.s1p2: The critical procurement insight: electricity is 60–70% of the cost of green hydrogen production. Green hydrogen discovered under SIGHT competitive bidding costs ₹397/kg for supply to IOCL refineries and ₹387/kg for BPCL/HPCL, and is expected to fall towards ₹260–310/kg as the scheme scales. The primary lever on that cost is the price of the solar power feeding the electrolyser. Cheaper solar means cheaper hydrogen. That is why every serious green hydrogen developer is either building or contracting for a large dedicated renewable plant — and why solar EPC contractors are the critical enabler of the entire value chain.
greenHydrogen.s2p1: SECI has run multiple SIGHT auctions across both components. Cumulatively, 19 companies now hold green hydrogen production allocations totalling 8,62,000 tonnes per annum, and 15 firms hold awards for roughly 3,000 MW of annual electrolyser manufacturing capacity. On the demand side, SECI has discovered prices for 7,24,000 MTPA of green ammonia supply to 13 fertiliser units. These are awarded contracts moving into execution — not proposals.
greenHydrogen.s2p2: The counterweight is equally important to understand before you build a business plan around it: as of February 2026, only about 8,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen capacity had actually been commissioned, against 8,62,000 TPA awarded. Awarded is not built. The gap between the two is exactly where EPC execution capacity sits over the next three to five years.

greenHydrogen.s3p1: For most small and mid-size EPCs, direct green hydrogen projects are not an immediate market. The projects are large, the clients are industrial conglomerates, and pre-qualification is demanding. That is an honest assessment — and it should shape how you position rather than whether you engage.

levels.title: Level 1 — Direct: dedicated renewable energy zones (large EPC firms)
levels.body: Electrolyser-linked solar parks under NGHM are driving ultra-large project tenders, typically 500 MW to multi-GW plants co-located with or near electrolyser facilities. The capability required — large-scale ground-mount, grid interconnection, HV evacuation, BESS integration — is beyond most mid-size contractors today. It is a growth target, not a current addressable market, for firms building toward that scale.

levels.title: Level 2 — Indirect: industrial captive solar for GH2 users (all EPC firms)
levels.body: Industrial clients evaluating green hydrogen — large manufacturers, fertiliser producers, refineries — need substantial captive solar as part of the same energy strategy. An EPC who understands the hydrogen connection can open a conversation about long-term energy procurement rather than a one-off rooftop installation.

greenHydrogen.s3p2: This is the more immediate opportunity. A fertiliser plant or refinery evaluating green hydrogen needs captive solar now — to reduce its electricity cost baseline and its emissions profile. The contractor who positions as a renewable energy partner for industrial decarbonisation, rather than as an installer, wins larger and longer contracts.

greenHydrogen.s4p1: Green hydrogen-linked solar is categorically different in scale from commercial rooftop or standard ground-mount EPC. Understanding what procurement looks like at each tier is the first step toward qualifying for it.
